correctness.rationale: For pairs of old points at distance 1 the only forbidden new distance pair is {1,3}; at old distance 3 the only forbidden pair is (1,1). Thus all coordinates are in {2,3}, or the unique class with a 1 has only 1s and 2s and all others use 2 and 3. The extension and homogeneity properties realize and separate exactly these labeled types, proving the polynomial. Evaluating y=1,z=0 gives 1+Σ_s m_s((1+x)^s−1); its triangular coefficient transform determines every multiplicity m_s. An independently written exhaustive multiplicity recursion covered all positive partitions through 16. It evaluated the scalar via a geometric sum (case split by the first 1 in an active class) and compared all colliding partition pairs. It confirmed the unique n=10 unrestricted pair at 4864 and the two n=16 same-k pairs at (k,N)=(5,339968),(6,385024); neither grouping produced an earlier collision. Adding one common positive part t sends the scalar to 2^t N+(2^t−1)2^n, keeps the partitions distinct, and preserves equality of k if required, proving the all-larger assertions.
residual_risks: The finite census is bounded at 16 and is not used as a proof of general identities. Types are in the ordinary metric ambient space with all three positive distances, not in the category of ultrametric extensions.

value.rationale: The scalar-versus-refined comparison answers a reconstruction question for a natural family of homogeneous-metric parameter sets. The result identifies exactly how early scalar information is lost, how much of that loss remains even when the class count is given, and why the refined invariant avoids it. The independent n=10 different-k witness, exact all-k first-layer census and persistence separate its contribution from a fresh computation of the known five-class pair alone.
residual_risks: No all-arity or arbitrary-ultrametric reconstruction statement is supported.
